title: Atlas Insurance customer story (v0 outline) — Document summarization + RAG migration
content:
Working title options (pick 1)
- “Atlas Insurance cut claim-review turnaround time with low-latency document summarization + RAG on Redwood Inference”
- “How Atlas Insurance migrated enterprise summarization to Redwood for predictable latency and lower $/1M tokens”
- “From provider X to Redwood: Atlas Insurance improves reliability and controls inference costs for document workflows”

One-liner summary (draft)
Atlas Insurance powers an internal claims and underwriting workflow that summarizes long policy/claim documents and retrieves supporting evidence via RAG. After hitting reliability and cost volatility with their prior inference provider, Atlas migrated to Redwood Inference to meet strict latency targets, reduce unit costs, and add an evaluation harness to prevent regressions.

Customer snapshot (to confirm)
- Company: Atlas Insurance (enterprise insurance provider)
- Audience: VP Eng, Head of Data/ML Platform, Claims Ops leadership
- Deployment mode: TBD (likely Dedicated; confirm if any VPC requirements)
- Primary use case: Document summarization + RAG (internal app used by adjusters/underwriters)
- Key models: TBD (open model via Redwood catalog; confirm if they pinned model version)

Primary story angle
1) Migration from another inference provider (stability + transparency + control)
2) Hit latency SLOs for “human-in-the-loop” workflows (p95 matters more than average)
3) Better unit economics ($/1M tokens) through batching/caching + routing policies
4) Instituted evaluation harness + prompt sets to guard quality during optimization/model upgrades

Redwood messaging pillars to emphasize (map to approved claims)
- Performance economics: concrete levers and measured outcomes (batching, caching, quantization profiles if used)
- Reliability + graceful degradation: fallbacks, retries, routing policies, regional capacity behavior
- Deployment flexibility: Dedicated for predictable throughput and isolation (or Private if needed)
- Operational tooling: Console dashboards, token-level breakdowns, error analysis, rollout controls

Outline (public case study page)

1) Problem: high-stakes document workflows with strict latency + cost constraints
- Context: Atlas processes large volumes of semi-structured documents (policies, adjuster notes, claim attachments, correspondence).
- The product experience: an internal assistant generates:
  - concise summaries (key facts, dates, parties, coverage)
  - suggested next actions
  - citations/evidence snippets via RAG (retrieval from internal corpus)
- Constraints:
  - p95 latency matters (analyst/adjuster waiting in the loop)
  - bursty traffic (end-of-month / catastrophe events)
  - quality needs to be stable across model changes (compliance + operational risk)
  - budget targets (LLM spend must be predictable)

2) Why they changed: pain points with prior inference provider (keep this non-inflammatory)
- Symptoms (draft; validate with Atlas + AE):
  - latency variance at peak hours; occasional tail spikes
  - cost unpredictability when context length increased / usage scaled
  - limited visibility into what drove spend and failures
  - difficulty enforcing model version pinning / safe rollouts
- Migration trigger moment (need a specific incident/decision):
  - “we needed to lock down p95 for production” / “cost per case was trending up”

3) Solution: Redwood Inference architecture for summarization + RAG
(Include a simple diagram block in final; Markus/Simran to validate.)
- Flow (draft)
  1. Document ingestion + chunking (Atlas side)
  2. Embeddings + indexing (Atlas side; Redwood embeddings optional if used)
  3. Retrieval step (Atlas side; top-k passages)
  4. Prompt assembly with retrieved context + policies
  5. Redwood inference call for:
     - summary
     - structured fields (if they do this)
     - citations / evidence list
  6. Post-processing + UI
- Redwood components to call out (only what’s true):
  - Dedicated capacity for predictable throughput
  - routing/fallback policies for reliability (e.g., model variant fallback)
  - caching (prefix/KV) for repeated template prompts and common boilerplate
  - workload-aware batching to improve unit cost while holding latency SLO
  - Console dashboards: p95, error rates, token usage by route

4) Implementation: migration plan and rollout
- Timeline (rough; confirm)
  - Week 0–2: baseline measurement + shadow traffic
  - Week 2–4: pilot subset of users / canary
  - Week 4–6: ramp to majority traffic; deprecate prior provider
- Key choices/lessons
  - pinned model versions; established change control
  - defined latency budget by step (retrieval vs generation)
  - standardized prompts/templates for consistency

5) Evals: preventing quality regressions while optimizing for cost/latency
- What they measured (draft)
  - summarization fidelity (key fields present)
  - citation correctness (evidence supports summary)
  - hallucination rate / “unsupported claims”
  - refusal/guardrail behavior (if applicable)
- Evaluation harness references (make this concrete)
  - built a prompt set derived from historical cases
  - ran A/B comparisons between baseline model/provider and Redwood setup
  - gating criteria before enabling a rollout (e.g., no regression beyond threshold)
- Note: We can describe the methodology even if they won’t publish exact scores.

6) Results (placeholders; require proof + approval)
We need at least one of the following to publish; otherwise use ranges + “measured internally.”
- Latency
  - Target: p95 under ___ seconds for typical doc length (define doc length)
  - Result: p95 improved from ___ to ___ OR reduced variance / tail latency
- Cost
  - Target: $___ per 1M tokens (or cost per case)
  - Result: reduced $/1M tokens by ___% OR reduced cost per case by ___%
- Reliability
  - Target: uptime ___% and reduced error rate
  - Result: error rate down from ___ to ___; improved retry/fallback behavior
- Throughput
  - Requests/sec at peak, or time to process daily batch

Metrics table (draft template; fill later)
- Baseline (prior provider):
  - p50 latency: ___
  - p95 latency: ___
  - error rate/timeouts: ___
  - cost per 1M tokens: ___
  - notes: workload mix, doc length distribution, prompt size
- After Redwood:
  - p50 latency: ___
  - p95 latency: ___
  - error rate/timeouts: ___
  - cost per 1M tokens: ___
  - notes: Dedicated sizing, batching/caching settings

Proof sources we should request (internal only)
- Redwood Console screenshots (redacted): latency distribution, token usage by route
- Atlas measurement notes: how they computed baselines, sample size, time window
- Evals: prompt set summary + gating thresholds (high level)
- If competitor is mentioned: keep it generic (“prior provider”), unless Atlas explicitly requests naming

7) Quotes (need 2–3; one technical, one business)
Quote prompts to capture
- “We needed predictable p95 latency; average wasn’t enough.”
- “The migration was faster than expected; we could validate quality with evals before flipping traffic.”
- “Unit economics improved once we applied batching/caching + pinned rollouts.”
- “We finally had visibility into spend drivers at the route level.”
Targets (confirm)
- Champion: ML Platform Lead (technical)
- Exec sponsor: VP Engineering or Claims Ops leader (business impact)

8) Security / compliance notes (be conservative)
- If they require privacy language, keep it general:
  - no customer PII shared publicly
  - metrics may be ranges
  - deployment details may be generalized
- Confirm if any requirements: data residency, audit logs, retention, encryption/KMS (only include if validated)

9) CTA + sales enablement hooks
- CTA (web): “Talk to us about Dedicated/Private deployments” / “See how Redwood meets p95 latency targets”
- Sales talk track (internal):
  - “If you’re seeing tail latency or cost volatility on summarization/RAG workloads, here’s how Atlas approached measurement, migration, and eval gating.”
- Suggested use in late-stage deals:
  - attach 1-pager PDF + offer reference call (subject to Atlas reference limits)

Open questions / TODO (as of v0)
- Confirm deployment mode (Dedicated vs Private/VPC) and what we can name publicly.
- Confirm if Atlas will allow logo usage; if not, plan for anonymized version.
- Confirm if they will publish exact metrics vs ranges.
- Identify the clearest before/after comparison window (avoid cherry-picking).
- Determine what “latency target” means in their workflow (end-to-end vs generation-only).
- Nail the migration narrative: what specifically broke down with prior provider, without sounding like a takedown.
- Identify what parts of the eval harness are safe to describe publicly.

Next steps (owner / date)
- Ethan: draft 1-page narrative from this outline (target: 2025-10-24)
- Soojin: review messaging + claims checklist (target: 2025-10-25)
- Markus/Simran: validate architecture description + what we can diagram (target: 2025-10-25)
- Avery/Rachel: confirm reference readiness + quote approvals path, and whether metrics can be shared as ranges (target: 2025-10-28)

Notes to self
- Keep tone developer-first and specific: concrete workflow, what was measured, what changed operationally.
- Avoid over-claiming (“guaranteed” / “always”); prefer “measured over X weeks” and “p95 improved by…”
- If we can’t publish hard numbers, emphasize process: Dedicated sizing + routing controls + eval gating + observability.
